objectives: Explain the difference between demand and quantity demanded, and between supply and quantity supplied.
Describe the law of demand and the law of supply as relationships between price and quantity.
Distinguish a movement along a curve (caused by a price change) from a shift of the curve itself (caused by other factors), and identify those factors.

concepts.definition: The whole relationship between each possible price and the amount consumers are willing and able to buy at that price. It can be shown as a table (demand schedule) or a graph (demand curve).
The amount consumers want to buy at one specific price. It is a single point on the demand curve.
Other things being equal, when the price rises, quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, quantity demanded rises.
Supply is the whole relationship between each possible price and the amount producers are willing to sell. Quantity supplied is the amount they want to sell at one specific price.
Other things being equal, when the price rises, quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls, quantity supplied falls.

concepts.term: Movement along a curve vs. shift of the curve
concepts.definition: A change in the good's own price moves you along the same curve (a change in quantity demanded or quantity supplied). A change in any other factor shifts the whole curve (a change in demand or supply).

concepts.term: Factors that shift demand and supply
concepts.definition: Demand: income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes, population, and expectations about the future. Supply: production costs, natural conditions such as weather, technology, and taxes, subsidies, and regulations.

beginner.summary: When a price goes up, buyers want to buy less and sellers want to sell more. But when something other than the price changes, like the weather or a new trend, how much people want to buy changes too.

sections.heading: Demand: wanting to buy and being able to
paragraphs: Picture a pizza place near your school. Would you buy a slice as often at $5 as you would at $3? Most people buy less, or pick a different snack, when the price goes up. The idea that people buy less as the price rises is called the law of demand.

Demand is the full list of how much people would buy at every price. Quantity demanded is the amount at just one of those prices. For example, "At $3 a slice, your class would buy 30 slices" describes a quantity demanded.

sections.heading: Supply: wanting to sell
paragraphs: Sellers see things the other way around. If the pizza place can charge more per slice, it will want to buy more ingredients and bake more pizzas. The idea that the amount sellers offer (quantity supplied) rises as the price rises is called the law of supply.

sections.heading: When the price changes vs. when something else changes
paragraphs: If only the price of a slice changes, people stick to their usual plans and just buy a little more or a little less.

But suppose exams end and you hang out with friends more often (a change in tastes or circumstances), your allowance goes up (a change in income), or a new burger place opens nearby (a substitute). Then the amount you want to buy changes even at the same price. We say that demand has changed.
The same goes for sellers. If cheese gets more expensive, or a drought makes ingredients scarce, the pizza place will make fewer pizzas even at the same price. We say that supply has changed.

intermediate.summary: The demand curve slopes down to the right, and the supply curve slopes up to the right. A price change causes a movement along a curve, while a change in any other factor shifts the entire curve.

sections.heading: Demand schedules and demand curves
paragraphs: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded. A table of that relationship is a demand schedule, and a graph of it is a demand curve. By convention, economists put price (P) on the vertical axis and quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis.

Because of the law of demand, the demand curve slopes down to the right. The assumption that other things stay the same (ceteris paribus) matters here: only by changing the price alone can we isolate the relationship between price and quantity demanded.

sections.heading: Supply schedules and supply curves
paragraphs: The supply curve shows that quantity supplied is larger at higher prices, so it slopes up to the right. As production expands, the cost of making one more unit usually rises, because producers must pay more for materials, hire extra workers, or use less suitable land and equipment. A higher price makes this more costly extra output worth producing, so producers increase the quantity supplied.

sections.heading: Change in quantity demanded vs. change in demand
paragraphs: When the good's own price changes, the point moves along the curve. This is a change in quantity demanded (or quantity supplied). When a factor other than price changes, the whole curve shifts to the right (an increase) or to the left (a decrease). This is a change in demand (or supply).

Factors that shift demand: income (for a normal good, higher income increases demand; for an inferior good, it decreases demand), prices of substitutes and complements, tastes and trends, the size and makeup of the population, and expectations about future prices.

Factors that shift supply: production costs such as raw materials and wages, natural conditions such as weather, production technology, and government policies such as taxes, subsidies, and regulations.

advanced.summary: Writing demand and supply as linear functions, Qd = a − bP and Qs = c + dP, the slopes measure how strongly quantity responds to price, and a change in an intercept represents a shift of the curve.

sections.heading: The demand function
paragraphs: As a function, demand can be written Qd = a − bP (a > 0, b > 0). The law of demand is the condition b > 0, that is, ΔQd/ΔP = −b < 0. Plugging in a specific price P₀ gives Qd(P₀), the quantity demanded at that price.
Market demand is the sum of individual consumers' quantities demanded at each price (a horizontal sum). So when the number of consumers grows, the market demand curve shifts to the right.

sections.heading: The supply function
paragraphs: Writing supply as Qs = c + dP (d > 0), the law of supply is the condition ΔQs/ΔP = d > 0. The intercept c can be read as a summary of non-price conditions such as costs and technology.

sections.heading: Shift factors and changes in the function
paragraphs: When the price changes, the function stays the same; we simply read a different point on it. When income, prices of related goods, tastes, population, or expectations change, a changes (and sometimes b as well), so the demand curve shifts. For example, if a rises from 100 to 130, quantity demanded increases by 30 at every price.
On the supply side, higher production costs, bad weather, or a new tax reduce c (a leftward shift), while better technology or a subsidy increases c (a rightward shift).
Real-world demand and supply are not guaranteed to be straight lines. Keep in mind that a linear model is an approximation that simplifies the relationship over a narrow range of prices.

worked_examples.title: Reading a demand schedule
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: The demand schedule for juice at a school snack bar shows 50 bottles a day at $1.00, 40 bottles at $1.50, and 30 bottles at $2.00. If the price rises from $1.00 to $2.00, by how many bottles does the daily quantity demanded fall?
worked_examples.answer: It falls by 20 bottles. The price rose and quantity demanded fell, which matches the law of demand.

worked_examples.title: Movement along the curve, or a shift of the curve?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: (A) Strawberries get cheaper, so people buy more strawberries. (B) Summer arrives, and people buy more ice cream even at the same price. (C) Fertilizer gets more expensive, so farmers bring less lettuce to market even at the same price. What kind of change is each one?
steps: (A) The good's own price changed → a movement along the demand curve (an increase in quantity demanded).
(B) A non-price factor (the season, tastes) changed → the demand curve shifts to the right (an increase in demand).
(C) A production cost rose → the supply curve shifts to the left (a decrease in supply).
worked_examples.answer: (A) a change in quantity demanded, (B) a change in demand (an increase), (C) a change in supply (a decrease)

worked_examples.title: Calculating quantity demanded from a linear demand function
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: Suppose demand in a regional rice market is Qd = 120 − 4P, where P is the price in dollars per 10-kg bag and Q is in thousands of bags. What is quantity demanded when the price rises from 10 to 15?
steps: A price increase of 5 lowered quantity demanded by 20. This matches the slope of −4.
worked_examples.answer: Quantity demanded is 60 thousand bags (down 20 thousand bags from 80 thousand).

graphs.title: An increase in demand: the demand curve shifts right
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example. If higher incomes make people want to buy 30 more units at every price, the demand curve shifts from D1 to D2. At the same price of 20, quantity demanded rises from 60 to 90 (a shift of the curve itself). You will learn how demand and supply together set the price (equilibrium) in Lesson 2.

graphs.title: A decrease in supply: the supply curve shifts left
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example. If higher raw-material costs make producers offer 20 fewer units at every price, the supply curve shifts from S1 to S2. At the same price of 40, quantity supplied falls from 50 to 30.

real_world_examples.title: Weather and the supply of farm products
paragraphs: Natural conditions such as droughts, heavy rain, and cold snaps are classic examples of factors that shift the supply of farm products. When harvests shrink, less reaches the market at every price, so the supply curve shifts to the left.
On the other hand, new farming techniques and improved crop varieties let farmers grow more at the same cost, which shifts the supply curve to the right.

sdg_case.title: A drought year: grain markets and food security
paragraphs: SDG 2 aims to end hunger and make sure everyone has enough safe, nutritious food all year round. SDG target 2.c calls for well-functioning food markets and timely access to market information, including information on food reserves, to help limit extreme price swings.

Hypothetical situation: A drought has sharply reduced a country's grain harvest. The supply curve shifts to the left, so the price rises, and households that spend a large share of their income on food are hit hardest. Compare the options the government could choose and the reasoning behind each.

options.name: Release government grain reserves onto the market
benefits: Adds to supply and can limit how much the price rises.
costs: Buying and storing reserves in advance costs money.
Once the reserves are used up, the country is less prepared for the next shock.
assumptions: Reserves are large enough, and officials can judge the right time to release them.

options.name: Let market prices adjust and publish information openly
benefits: High prices signal farmers to grow more and traders to import more.
costs: While prices are high, low-income households risk not getting enough to eat.
assumptions: Supply can recover fairly quickly through imports or the next harvest.

options.name: Give low-income households direct help with food costs
benefits: Protects food access for the most vulnerable households.
Keeps the market price signal in place.
costs: Costs public money, plus administrative costs to target the right households.
If supply does not change, the extra demand can push prices even higher.
assumptions: The government can identify eligible households accurately and pay them quickly.

discussion: If the government used all three options together, what order and combination would work best? Which assumptions does your answer depend on?

key_takeaways: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded; quantity demanded is the amount at one price. Supply and quantity supplied follow the same distinction.
Other things being equal, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, while price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
A price change causes a movement along a curve; a change in any non-price factor shifts the curve itself.
